Equations, linear relationships, systems, polynomials, rational expressions, radicals, and functions—built as one connected toolkit.
Translate algebraic structure, simplify without changing value, and solve equations with a reliable sequence of reversible moves.
Terms combine only when their variable parts match exactly. The coefficients change; the variable structure does not.
Distribution is multiplication across a sum. It expands an expression without changing its value—and it works in reverse when factoring.
Replace every occurrence of the variable, preserve the expression's grouping, and simplify only after the substitution is complete.
Parentheses and exponents set the structure; multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction then move left to right within their own level.
An equation stays true when the same legal operation is applied to both sides. Simplify, isolate, and check.
Either side can work. Choose the direction that keeps the variable coefficient positive and the arithmetic easy to audit.
Read slope as a rate, build equations from data, and connect tables, graphs, and formulas without treating them as separate topics.
Find the slope first, anchor it to either point, then convert forms only if the problem needs a different presentation.
Use intercepts when they are clean, or solve for y when slope and vertical change are more informative.
The intercept is the modeled output at input zero; the slope is the predicted change in output per unit of input. Context decides whether either interpretation is sensible.
Parallel nonvertical lines share a slope. Perpendicular nonvertical lines have slopes whose product is −1—but vertical and horizontal lines need separate language.
Use point-slope form when a point and slope are given; use slope-intercept form when the intercept or a quick graph is the main goal.
Slope measures how much the output changes for each one-unit change in the input. Its sign, size, and units all carry meaning.
Control exponents, multiply cleanly, and recognize the factor patterns that make higher-degree algebra manageable.
Add the exact term that turns a quadratic expression into a perfect-square trinomial, while preserving the equation's value.
The rules are compressed descriptions of repeated multiplication. Knowing where they come from prevents powers from spreading across sums illegally.
For x² + bx + c, find two numbers with product c and sum b. For ax² + bx + c, split the middle term using product ac.
The GCF is the largest expression dividing every term. Removing it first exposes the smaller polynomial that actually needs attention.
Every term in one factor multiplies every term in the other. Organize the products, then combine like terms once.
Recognize the pattern from term count, signs, square roots, and the middle coefficient—then expand to confirm rather than trusting appearance alone.
Move between radical and exponent notation, solve carefully, and use function language to describe inputs, outputs, and inverses.
Separate the starting amount from the repeated growth factor, then connect each parameter to a real change per time interval.
f(x) names the output of function f at input x. The parentheses indicate evaluation, not multiplication.
f⁻¹ reverses a function's input-output pairing; 1/f takes reciprocal outputs. They are generally different operations.
The denominator names the root and the numerator names the power. This notation lets radical expressions use the ordinary exponent rules.
Factor the radicand into a perfect power times what remains. Pull only complete groups through the radical bar.
Isolate one radical, raise both sides to the matching power, solve, and check every candidate in the original equation.
Track restrictions, simplify factors legally, combine fractions, and solve equations without losing excluded values.
Factor denominators, build the least common denominator, rewrite every numerator, then combine while preserving restrictions.
Direct variation keeps a constant ratio y/x; inverse variation keeps a constant product xy. The data pattern decides the model.
A rational expression is undefined wherever its original denominator is zero. Simplifying the formula does not restore an excluded input.
Treat the stacked fraction as division, state every original restriction, and clear the small denominators with one common multiplier.
Factor completely, record excluded inputs, and cancel common factors. Individual terms separated by addition cannot be canceled.
List restrictions, multiply every term by the least common denominator, solve the resulting equation, and reject candidates outside the original domain.
Solve simultaneous conditions, choose an efficient method, and describe whole solution regions instead of isolated numbers.
Choose from the equation structure: graph when the intersection matters visually, substitute when a variable is already isolated, and eliminate when coefficients align.
Solve each condition, reverse the inequality only when multiplying or dividing by a negative, then combine by intersection or union.
Align like terms, create opposite coefficients, add the equations, and recover the variable that was deliberately removed.
Draw the boundary, decide whether it belongs to the solution, then test a point to choose the correct half-plane.
For two linear equations, the coefficient pattern determines whether the graphs intersect once, never meet, or are actually the same line.
Replace one variable with an equal expression, solve the resulting one-variable equation, then recover and verify the second coordinate.
